title: Chinese Cinderella
author: Adeline Yen Mah
blurb: A neglected daughter finally wins her father’s approval through success at school in 1950s Hong Kong.
source: A neglected daughter wins her father's approval through academic success
heading: From Chinese Cinderella - Adeline Yen Mah
context: Growing up in a wealthy family in 1950s Hong Kong, Mah should have had an enviable childhood, but she was rejected by her dominating stepmother and despised by her brothers and sisters. She was sent to a boarding school and left there. In this extract from her autobiography she relates one of the few occasions when she went home.

paragraphs.html: Time went by relentlessly and it was Saturday again. Eight weeks more and it would be the end of term ... in my case perhaps the end of school forever.

Four of us were playing Monopoly. My heart was not in it and I was losing steadily. Outside it was hot and there was a warm wind blowing. The radio warned of a possible typhoon the next day. It was my turn and I threw the dice. As I played, the thought of leaving school throbbed at the back of my mind like a persistent toothache.
'Adeline!' Ma-mien Valentino was calling.
'You can't go now,' Mary protested. 'For once I'm winning. One, two, three, four. Good! You've landed on my property. Thirty-five dollars, please. Oh, good afternoon, Mother Valentino!'
We all stood up and greeted her.
'Adeline, didn't you hear me call you? Hurry up downstairs! Your chauffeur is waiting to take you home!'
Full of foreboding, I ran downstairs as in a nightmare, wondering who had died this time. Father's chauffeur assured me everyone was healthy.
'Then why are you taking me home?' I asked.
'How should I know?' he answered defensively, shrugging his shoulders. 'Your guess is as good as mine. They give the orders and I carry them out.'
During the short drive home, my heart was full of dread and I wondered what I had done wrong. Our car stopped at an elegant villa at mid-level, halfway up the hill between the peak and the harbour.
'Where are we?' I asked foolishly.
'Don't you know anything?' the chauffeur replied rudely. 'This is your new home. Your parents moved here a few months ago.'
'I had forgotten,' I said as I got out.
Ah Gum opened the door. Inside, it was quiet and cool.
'Where is everyone?'
'Your mother is out playing bridge. Your two brothers and Little Sister are sunbathing by the swimming-pool. Your father is in his room and wants to see you as soon as you get home.'
'See me in his room?' I was overwhelmed by the thought that I had been summoned by Father to enter the Holy of Holies — a place to which I had never been invited. Why? ...

Timidly, I knocked on the door. Father was alone, looking relaxed in his slippers and bathrobe, reading a newspaper. He smiled as I entered and I saw he was in a happy mood. I breathed a small sigh of relief at first but became uneasy again when I wondered why he was being so nice, thinking, Is this a giant ruse on his part to trick me? Dare I let my guard down?
'Sit down! Sit down!' He pointed to a chair. 'Don't look so scared. Here, take a look at this! They're writing about someone we both know, I think.'
He handed me the day's newspaper and there, in one corner, I saw my name ADELINE YEN in capital letters prominently displayed.

'It was announced today that 14-year-old Hong Kong schoolgirl ADELINE JUN-LING YEN of Sacred Heart Canossian School, Caine Road, Hong Kong, has won first prize in the International Play-writing Competition held in London, England, for the 1951—1952 school year. It is the first time that any local Chinese student from Hong Kong has won such a prestigious event. Besides a medal, the prize comes with a cash reward of FIFTY ENGLISH POUNDS. Our sincere congratulations, ADELINE YEN, for bringing honour to Hong Kong. We are proud of you'.
Is it possible? Am I dreaming? Me, the winner?

'I was going up the lift this morning with my friend C.Y. Tung when he showed me this article and asked me, "Is the winner Adeline Jun-ling Yen related to you? The two of you have the same uncommon last name." Now C.Y. himself has a few children about your age but so far none of them has won an international literary prize, as far as I know. So I was quite pleased to tell him you are my daughter. Well done!'

He looked radiant. For once, he was proud of me. In front of his revered colleague, C.Y. Tung, a prominent fellow businessman also from Shanghai, I had given him face. I thought, Is this the big moment I have been waiting for? My whole being vibrated with all the joy in the world. I only had to stretch out my hand to reach the stars.
'Tell me, how did you do it?' he continued. 'How come you won?'

'Well, the rules and regulations were so very complicated. One really has to be dedicated just to understand what they want. Perhaps I was the only one determined enough to enter and there were no other competitors!'
He laughed approvingly. 'I doubt it very much but that's a good answer.'
'Please, Father,' I asked boldly, thinking it was now or never. 'May I go to university in England too, just like my brothers?'
'I do believe you have potential. Tell me, what would you study?'

My heart gave a giant lurch as it dawned on me that he was agreeing to let me go. How marvellous it was simply to be alive! Study? I thought. Going to England is like entering heaven. Does it matter what you do after you get to heaven?
But Father was expecting an answer. What about creative writing? After all, I had just won first prize in an international writing competition!
'I plan to study literature. I'll be a writer.'

'Writer!' he scoffed. 'You are going to starve! What language are you going to write in and who is going to read your writing? Though you may think you're an expert in both Chinese and English, your Chinese is actually rather elementary. As for your English, don't you think the native English speakers can write better than you?'
I waited in silence. I did not wish to contradict him.

'You will go to England with Third Brother this summer and you will go to medical school. After you graduate, you will specialise in obstetrics. Women will always be having babies. Women patients prefer women doctors. You will learn to deliver their babies. That's a foolproof profession for you. Don't you agree?'

Agree? Of course I agreed. Apparently, he had it all planned out. As long as he let me go to university in England, I would study anything he wished. How did that line go in Wordsworth's poem? Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive.
'Father, I shall go to medical school in England and become a doctor. Thank you very, very much.'

relentlessly.what: The first word of the extract gives time a will of its own. 'Relentlessly' means without pause or mercy, as if time is chasing her.
relentlessly.effect: We feel the weeks running out before we know why. Something bad is coming and she cannot slow it down.

perhaps-forever.quote: perhaps the end of school forever
perhaps-forever.what: The ellipsis (...) makes her pause before the worst thought. 'Forever' turns a normal end of term into a possible end to her education.
perhaps-forever.effect: We learn at once that school is her lifeline. 'Perhaps' shows she has no control: someone else will decide.

heart-not.quote: My heart was not in it
heart-not.what: She is playing a game with friends, yet her heart is 'not in it'. Her body is in the room and her thoughts are somewhere else.
heart-not.effect: An ordinary Saturday game shows how worry spoils even happy moments. We sense that her fear never really leaves her.

throbbed-toothache.quote: throbbed at the back of my mind like a persistent toothache
throbbed-toothache.what: Mah compares her fear of leaving school to 'a persistent toothache'. 'Throbbed' gives the worry a beat, like pain that pulses.
throbbed-toothache.effect: Everyone knows a toothache: you cannot ignore it or escape it. We feel her worry as a dull ache that will not go away.

chauffeur-waiting.quote: Your chauffeur is waiting to take you home!
chauffeur-waiting.what: Mother Valentino's exclamation breaks up the game. Being fetched home without warning starts the main action of the extract.
chauffeur-waiting.effect: For most children this would be good news. For Adeline it is alarming, which tells us that home is a place of danger.

full-foreboding.what: 'Foreboding' means a strong feeling that something bad will happen. She feels it before anyone has told her anything.
full-foreboding.effect: Her fear is automatic. We realise that, for her, a call from home has always meant trouble.

as-nightmare.what: She runs downstairs 'as in a nightmare'. The simile suggests a dream where you move helplessly towards something terrible.
as-nightmare.effect: We feel her panic and lack of control. The moment seems unreal to her, too frightening to take in.

who-died.what: The words 'this time' hint that she has been called home with news of a death before. A death is her first guess.
who-died.effect: The calm way she says it is shocking. We see how used she is to bad news and how little good she expects from home.

your-guess.quote: Your guess is as good as mine. They give the orders and I carry them out
your-guess.what: The chauffeur shrugs off her question. 'They give the orders' shows a household run by commands from the top.
your-guess.effect: Nobody explains anything to Adeline. She is as powerless and uninformed as the servants, which deepens our sense of her isolation.

heart-dread.quote: my heart was full of dread
heart-dread.what: Her heart is 'full of dread', as if fear has filled it to the top. She assumes at once that she has done something wrong.
heart-dread.effect: She blames herself before she knows the facts. We see a child trained to expect punishment.

foolishly.what: The adverb judges her own question. She calls herself foolish for not knowing where her family lives.
foolishly.effect: The real failure is her parents', who moved without telling her. Yet she takes the blame, showing how deeply she has absorbed their low opinion of her.

dont-know-anything.what: The chauffeur answers with a scornful question, and Mah adds that he replied 'rudely'. Even a paid driver feels free to mock her.
dont-know-anything.effect: Servants copy the way the family treats her. Her low place in the household is clear to everyone.

i-forgotten.what: Her parents moved months ago and she has never seen the new house. Her short reply takes the blame on herself.
i-forgotten.effect: Readers can see the truth she covers up: nobody told her or brought her home. Three quiet words hide real hurt.

father-room.quote: Your father is in his room and wants to see you as soon as you get home
father-room.what: Ah Gum says where each family member is and saves Father for last. He wants to see her 'as soon as you get home'.
father-room.effect: The urgency raises the stakes. Like Adeline, we expect a punishment and wait to find out what she has done.

holy-holies.what: The Holy of Holies was the inner room of the Temple in Jerusalem, which only the high priest could enter. Mah uses it for Father's bedroom.
holy-holies.effect: Father seems almost like a god: distant, powerful and out of reach. Being invited in is both an honour and a terror.

happy-mood.what: After all the build-up of fear, Father is relaxed and smiling. His 'happy mood' is the opposite of what she, and we, expected.
happy-mood.effect: The twist keeps us uneasy. His good mood is so rare that it feels strange, almost threatening.

small-sigh.what: 'Small' limits her relief. She lets go of a little fear, then the worry returns straight away.
small-sigh.effect: We see she cannot trust good moments with her father. Any kindness from him has to be checked for a catch.

giant-ruse.quote: Is this a giant ruse on his part to trick me? Dare I let my guard down?
giant-ruse.what: A 'ruse' is a trick. Her two questions show her mind racing to test his kindness, and 'Dare' makes relaxing sound risky.
giant-ruse.effect: It is sad that a smile from her own father feels like a trap. We understand how much harm years of rejection have done.

dont-scared.what: Father gives her a command (an imperative). Her fear shows on her face, and he notices it.
dont-scared.effect: His tone is kind, yet it is still an order. He seems unaware that he is the reason she is scared.

adeline-capitals.quote: ADELINE YEN in capital letters prominently displayed
adeline-capitals.what: Mah copies the newspaper's capitals, so her name jumps off our page just as it jumped off his.
adeline-capitals.effect: A girl ignored at home is suddenly picked out in public. The capitals show how huge this moment of being noticed is.

prestigious-event.what: The newspaper's formal words, like 'prestigious' (highly respected), mark this as a public honour. She is the first local Chinese student to win.
prestigious-event.effect: This is exactly the kind of success Father's world values. We start to see why his attitude to her changes.

fifty-pounds.what: The prize money is printed in capitals, just like her name. Fifty pounds was a great deal of money for a schoolgirl in the 1950s.
fifty-pounds.effect: Money is something Father, a businessman, understands. The capitals hint that this detail will matter to him as much as the honour.

bringing-honour.what: The newspaper says her win brings honour to Hong Kong. One girl's success is shared by the whole community.
bringing-honour.effect: The same idea matters at home. If her success honours Hong Kong, it can also honour her family, which is what Father cares about.

is-possible.quote: Is it possible? Am I dreaming? Me, the winner?
is-possible.what: Three short questions come in a rush. The last, 'Me, the winner?', is barely a sentence, as if she cannot finish the thought.
is-possible.effect: We share her shock. Someone so used to being treated as worthless cannot believe she has won.

well-done.what: Father ends a long story about his friend C.Y. Tung with two words of praise. Most of his speech is about his own pride.
well-done.effect: To Adeline these words mean everything. Sharp readers may notice the praise comes because she has made him look good.

radiant.what: 'Radiant' means shining or glowing. Father seems to give off light, a huge change from the cold figure we expected.
radiant.effect: His pleasure lights her up too. The single word shows how completely his mood controls hers.

for-once.quote: For once, he was proud of me
for-once.what: 'For once' tells us this has never happened before. The short sentence sits at the centre of the extract as its turning point.
for-once.effect: Two small words sum up a lifetime of rejection. The joy is real, and so is the sadness behind it.

given-face.what: In Chinese culture 'face' means respect and reputation. Her prize has raised Father's standing in front of an important fellow businessman.
given-face.effect: Her value to him seems to depend on what she does for his image. We may feel uneasy that his pride is partly about himself.

whole-being.quote: My whole being vibrated with all the joy in the world
whole-being.what: 'Vibrated' makes joy a physical force shaking her. 'All the joy in the world' is hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration).
whole-being.effect: The exaggeration matches how a child feels at a moment like this. After so much fear, the happiness is overwhelming.

stretch-stars.quote: I only had to stretch out my hand to reach the stars
stretch-stars.what: The stars stand for her biggest hopes. 'Only had to stretch out my hand' makes them feel easy to reach for the first time.
stretch-stars.effect: We share her soaring hope. We may also sense danger: hopes raised this high have a long way to fall.

only-one.quote: Perhaps I was the only one determined enough to enter and there were no other competitors!
only-one.what: She jokes that she won because nobody else entered. Self-deprecation (making fun of yourself) stops her seeming boastful.
only-one.effect: She knows modesty is the safe way to handle Father. The joke shows a clever, careful girl who has learned to protect herself.

doubt-it.quote: I doubt it very much but that's a good answer
doubt-it.what: Father laughs and praises her 'good answer'. He seems to like her modesty as much as her prize.
doubt-it.effect: This relaxed exchange is the closest they come to warmth. We see that she earns approval by being humble and pleasing him.

now-never.what: She sees that his rare good mood is her one chance. The idiom shows her thinking fast and deciding to be bold.
now-never.effect: Tension rises again as we wait for his answer. Everything she wants hangs on a single question.

may-i-go.quote: May I go to university in England too, just like my brothers?
may-i-go.what: She asks to go to England 'just like my brothers'. The word 'too' shows the brothers' places are already settled.
may-i-go.effect: Her request exposes the unfairness in the family. The boys get a university education without asking, while she has to plead for it.

have-potential.quote: I do believe you have potential
have-potential.what: 'Potential' means ability that could grow. Father praises what she might become, then moves straight on to questions.
have-potential.effect: Even his warmest words hold something back. She still has to prove herself to earn his full respect.

heart-lurch.quote: My heart gave a giant lurch
heart-lurch.what: A 'lurch' is a sudden, jerky movement. 'Giant' stresses its force as she realises he is saying yes.
heart-lurch.effect: We feel the jolt with her. Her body reacts before her mind has fully caught up with the news.

how-marvellous.quote: How marvellous it was simply to be alive!
how-marvellous.what: The exclamation celebrates simply being alive. Earlier the same afternoon she ran downstairs wondering who had died.
how-marvellous.effect: The contrast shows how far her feelings have swung. It also hints at how low she has felt before this moment.

entering-heaven.quote: Going to England is like entering heaven. Does it matter what you do after you get to heaven?
entering-heaven.what: She compares going to England to entering heaven. Her question suggests the subject does not matter once you get there.
entering-heaven.effect: England means escape from a home where she is unloved. We sense how unhappy her life is if leaving feels like heaven.

writer-scoffed.quote: Writer!' he scoffed. 'You are going to starve!
writer-scoffed.what: Father throws the word 'Writer!' back at her. 'Scoffed' means mocked, and the threat that she will 'starve' treats her dream as foolish.
writer-scoffed.effect: Her joy is cut short at once. He dismisses the very talent that won the prize he is so proud of.

rather-elementary.quote: your Chinese is actually rather elementary
rather-elementary.what: Father calls her Chinese 'rather elementary', meaning basic. Next he doubts her English as well.
rather-elementary.effect: He leaves her no language to write in. By undermining her confidence, he clears the way for his own plan.

waited-silence.quote: I waited in silence. I did not wish to contradict him
waited-silence.what: Two short, flat sentences follow Father's long speech. She says nothing, though her dream has just been crushed.
waited-silence.effect: Her silence says a lot. We see a girl who has learned that arguing with Father is never safe.

medical-school.quote: you will go to medical school
medical-school.what: Father repeats 'you will' as he sets out her future: England, medical school, then obstetrics. Each step is an order.
medical-school.effect: Her prize has won her the chance to go to England. Her career, however, is chosen for her.

foolproof-profession.quote: That's a foolproof profession for you. Don't you agree?
foolproof-profession.what: 'Don't you agree?' sounds like a question, yet only one answer is allowed. 'Foolproof' means certain to succeed.
foolproof-profession.effect: He pretends to ask her opinion after deciding everything. We see how little real choice she has.

agree-course.what: She picks up his word 'agree' and answers it at once. Her reply turns his rhetorical question into a plain statement.
agree-course.effect: There may be a trace of irony (saying one thing while hinting at another). Refusing could cost her England, so agreeing is the only safe answer.

apparently-planned.quote: Apparently, he had it all planned out
apparently-planned.what: 'Apparently' shows her slowly realising that Father had already decided. Her own wishes were never part of the plan.
apparently-planned.effect: We sense the limits of her victory. She is free to leave home, yet he still controls her from a distance.

bliss-dawn.quote: Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive
bliss-dawn.what: She quotes the poet Wordsworth, who wrote this line about the hope of the French Revolution. Her 'dawn' is the start of a new life.
bliss-dawn.effect: Moments after Father mocked her writing, she reaches for poetry. It quietly proves she has the literary mind he dismissed.

father-shall.quote: Father, I shall go to medical school in England and become a doctor. Thank you very, very much
father-shall.what: Her final words are polite and formal ('I shall'). She repeats his plan back to him word for word.
father-shall.effect: The doubled 'very' shows real gratitude. It is also sad: she thanks him for a future he chose, giving up writing to escape.

obstetrics.meaning: The branch of medicine that cares for women in pregnancy and childbirth.
obstetrics.note: Father picks this exact specialism for her before she has even started medical school.
obstetrics.effect: His reason is that 'Women will always be having babies'. Even within medicine, he limits her to work he thinks suits a woman.

overview.heading: Why Mah wrote this
overview.intro: Mah shows what it was like to be an unwanted daughter.

points.label: To show neglect
points.text: "I had forgotten" shows how completely she was left out of family life.

points.label: To explain Chinese values
points.text: "I had given him face" shows that her worth to Father is tied to his reputation.

points.label: To show limits on girls
points.text: "That's a foolproof profession for you" shows Father choosing a career he thinks suits a girl.

overview.heading: Who she is writing for
overview.intro: Mah writes for several kinds of reader.

points.label: Readers new to Chinese culture
points.text: "I had given him face" and the Hong Kong setting open a window on a different culture.

points.label: Anyone wanting a parent's approval
points.text: "For once, he was proud of me" captures a longing almost every reader recognises.

points.label: Young women facing limits
points.text: "May I go to university in England too" speaks to girls who have had to fight for equal chances.

overview.heading: How her tone changes
overview.intro: Her voice moves from fear, to joy, to quiet acceptance.

points.label: Fearful child
points.text: "Full of foreboding" shows a girl who expects punishment whenever she is called home.

points.label: Disbelieving winner
points.text: "Is it possible? Am I dreaming?" shows she cannot believe good news about herself.

points.label: Joyful daughter
points.text: "My heart gave a giant lurch" shows joy so strong she feels it in her body.

points.label: Obedient survivor
points.text: "Of course I agreed" shows her accepting Father's plan so she can still escape.

overview.heading: Language choices
overview.intro: Mah uses images that let us feel her emotions.

points.label: Feelings made physical
points.text: "like a persistent toothache" turns her worry into a pain we all know.

points.label: Religious imagery
points.text: "Holy of Holies" and "entering heaven" make Father seem god-like and England seem like paradise.

points.label: Reaching for the stars
points.text: "stretch out my hand to reach the stars" shows her dreams suddenly within reach.

points.label: Literary allusion
points.text: "Bliss was it in that dawn" borrows Wordsworth's words and proves her love of literature.

overview.heading: How it is organised
overview.intro: The extract swings from dread to triumph, then to compromise.

points.label: Fear to triumph
points.text: "Your chauffeur is waiting" starts a tension that the prize news suddenly releases.

points.label: Turning point
points.text: "For once, he was proud of me" marks the moment everything changes between them.

points.label: Dream refused, plan imposed
points.text: "you will go to medical school" replaces her writing dream with Father's plan.

points.label: Grateful ending
points.text: "Thank you very, very much" ends the extract with her accepting the compromise.
